title: It’s a best practice - why isn’t it working?!
author: Jenny R. Allen
summary: Allen recalls being promoted to director with a mental file of 'Things I Will Never Do as a Manager' and a bucketful of best practices she was sure would work. Her first weekly 1:1s failed badly: one report read a list of accomplishments without looking up, another had nothing to say, and she blamed them rather than her plan. She had inherited a team that rarely held 1:1s and never explained what hers were for, so they assumed she wanted to keep tabs on them. Once she explained the purpose, offered prompts and asked a 'magic wand' question, the meetings began to produce real information. She frames this as tool bias, letting a solution define the problem, and concludes that best practices are success stories tied to a particular problem in a particular context.
points: Tool bias means reaching for a proven practice before understanding the team's history, context and actual problem.
A practice introduced without an explanation of its purpose will be filled in with the team's own, often suspicious, assumptions.
Blaming people for the failure of your best practice is a signal to question the practice and the rollout instead.
Concrete prompts and one good question, such as what one thing you would take off their plate, can unlock a stalled conversation.
Before adopting a best practice, check whether you actually have the same problem it was built to solve.
quotes: I had a bucketful of hammers I couldn’t wait to use - before ever meeting the team I was to manage, let alone understanding their world.
Absent that explanation, the team made their own assumptions about why I wanted to meet with them weekly - mainly, she wants to keep tabs on us.

I’d thrown a bunch of 1:1s on the calendar, figuring my new employees would be jazzed to have a manager who wanted to engage on a regular basis. Scheduling them was one thing; explaining what they were for was the part I’d missed.
Best practices are success stories - that’s why we like them. But we sometimes forget that they’re based on a particular problem in a particular situation.
We rush to adopt a best practice without first determining if we have the same problem.
To get the ball rolling, I asked each one of them, “If I could wave a magic wand and take one thing off your plate, what would it be?
One of them is tool bias - letting a solution define the problem. You know - when you have a hammer, everything looks like a nail.
This was me blaming my new employees for the failure of my brilliant best practice.
